blocks.text: In Focus: The MFA Review: University of Arizona, School of Art
©David Taylor, Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging

Each installment of In Focus: The MFA Review highlights a different MFA program for photographic artists, offering readers a concise overview of its identity, curriculum, faculty, student experience, financial support, and post-graduation outcomes. It also serves as a showcase of the creative work produced by faculty, students, and alumni. Rather than functioning as rankings or endorsements, these features are intended as practical starting points—tools to help prospective students compare programs, identify what matters most to them, and make more informed decisions about their graduate education. While certain details shared in these articles may change over time, my hope is that these program snapshots offer a clear sense of what each represents in the present moment.
Thank you to David Taylor for completing this interview and compiling all the images/resources!
Institution name: University of Arizona, School of Art
Degree Title: MFA in Studio Art
Location: Tucson, AZ
Link to Program Page: https://art.arizona.edu
Link to Application Page: https://grad.arizona.edu
Instagram: @uazschoolofart / @uarizonaphoto
©David Taylor, Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging
Tell us a little about your program. How would you define its scope and purpose?

The Photography, Video and Imaging (PVI) area of the graduate program at the University of Arizona is a rigorous, research-driven MFA that supports the development of critically engaged, interdisciplinary artists. The program emphasizes conceptual depth, visual experimentation, and dialogue within contemporary art discourse. It prepares students for professional careers as artists, educators, and cultural producers.
©Martina Shenal, Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging
What would you say makes your program special?

PVI is distinguished by its integration within a major research university, its strong interdisciplinary ethos, and access to world-class resources such as the Center for Creative Photography. The program fosters a balance between conceptual rigor and material exploration, encouraging students to situate their work within broader social, political, and historical contexts. The program’s relatively small cohort size, with a 2:1 student faculty ratio, ensures close faculty mentorship and a collaborative peer environment.
©Martina Shenal, Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging
What specialized facilities are available for student use (i.e. darkroom, lighting studio, print lab)?

Students have access to extensive facilities including group and private analog darkrooms, alternative process facilities, digital imaging labs, professional lighting studios, large-format printing resources, video production suites and spaces for imaging—including projection mapping and work in computational image making. Facilities also include a well resourced “cage” with a wide range of equipment for still photography, video production, sound recording, location lighting, AR/VR work, 3D capture and more.
©Kaitlyn Jo Smith, Career-Track Lecturer, Photography, Video and Imaging
Is your program strictly photography-focused, or does it encourage/allow interdisciplinary work?

While historically rooted in lens-based practices, the PVI program strongly encourages interdisciplinary exploration. Students frequently integrate photography, video, installation, performance, sound, and emerging technologies into their work.
©Kaitlyn Jo Smith, Career-Track Lecturer, Photography, Video and Imaging
Do you specialize in a particular area (i.e. documentary, experimental, environmental work)? And once in the program, is a student able to shift their focus if their creative interests change?

The program does not prescribe a singular specialization; instead, it supports a wide array of practices including documentary, conceptual, experimental, and socially engaged work. Students are encouraged to evolve their practice over time, and shifting focus is fully supported as part of the research process.
©Marcos Serafim, Assistant Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging
How structured is the curriculum? Are there required courses, or is it more self-directed?

The 60 credit curriculum combines a core set of required seminars, critique and studio courses with a high degree of self-direction. Students develop individualized study plans in consultation with faculty, allowing them to tailor coursework to their evolving artistic goals. Graduates frequently pursue courses in other areas of the university to complement and expand their practice.
MFA Degree Requirements: here
©Marcos Serafim, Assistant Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging
Does the program incorporate video work or emerging media such as AI, VR/AR, or 3D/360 imaging?

The program actively supports video and time-based media, as well as experimental and emerging technologies. Students are encouraged to incorporate new media approaches—including computational and expanded imaging practices—into their work as appropriate to their research.
©Sama Alshaibi, Regents Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging (Program Chair)
Does the program offer career development support, such as portfolio reviews, workshop/conference attendance, or networking opportunities?

The program provides multiple forms of professional development through a dedicated course—ART 596A: Graduate Professional Practice, individual and group graduate critiques, exhibition opportunities, teaching experience, and support for conference participation. Students also benefit from engagement with curators, historians, critics, and artists through the School of Art Visiting Artists and Scholars Endowment (VASE) lecture series.
©Sama Alshaibi, Regents Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging (Program Chair)
What are key graduation requirements (exhibition, thesis paper, portfolio, etc.)?

Graduation requirements include a final thesis exhibition, participation in critiques and reviews throughout the program. Students also present their work publicly and complete a comprehensive body of work that demonstrates conceptual and technical development. Additionally, students may opt into a written MFA thesis component.
©Camille Trautman, MFA 2025
Who are your current faculty members? What are their areas of creative interest?
Sama Alshaibi — Regents Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging (Program Chair)

Sama Alshaibi is an Iraqi–Palestinian artist working across photography, video, and installation. Her practice explores the concept of aftermath—addressing war, exile, migration, and ecological crisis. She frequently uses her body within constructed works to challenge representations of gender and Middle Eastern identity. She is a Guggenheim Fellow, and her work has been exhibited internationally, including at the Venice Biennale and the Museum of Modern Art. https://www.samaalshaibi.com/
Marcos Serafim — Assistant Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging

Marcos Serafim is a Brazilian artist and documentarian working across video, sound, installation, and moving-image practices. His research examines tensions between data, media, and representation, often focusing on sociopolitical and technological conditions affecting marginalized subjects. His work has been exhibited internationally and screened at film festivals across multiple continents. https://marcosserafim.art/
Martina Shenal — Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging

Martina Shenal is a photographer whose work focuses on landscape and environmental transformation. Her projects engage issues such as climate change, wildfire, and ecological instability, often grounded in sustained fieldwork. She has received numerous fellowships and grants, including support from WESTAF/NEA and the Arizona Commission on the Arts, and exhibits internationally. https://www.martinashenal.com/
Kaitlyn Jo Smith — Career-Track Lecturer, Photography, Video and Imaging

Kaitlyn Jo Smith is an interdisciplinary artist whose work examines the impact of automation and emerging technologies on America’s working class. Drawing on her rural upbringing, her practice explores the intersections of labor, religion, and technological change through photography, installation, and machine learning. Her work has been exhibited nationally and internationally and has received multiple awards, including the Alice C. Cole Fellowship. https://www.kaitlynjosmith.com/
David Taylor — Professor, Photography, Video and Imaging

David Taylor’s photographic and multimedia installation work examines place, territory, and political geography, with a focus on the U.S.–Mexico border. His long-term projects explore how borders change over time and operate as expansive systems. A Guggenheim Fellow and recipient of a 2026 Graham Foundation grant, his work is held in numerous collections including the MFA Houston, Universidad Autónima de Baja California (UABC) and the Library of Congress. https://www.dtaylorphoto.com
©Camille Trautman, MFA 2025
Are faculty members primarily full-time or adjunct?
Full-time
How involved are faculty in mentoring students beyond coursework?

Faculty maintain a strong commitment to mentorship through regular studio visits, critiques, and thesis advising. The small cohort model allows for sustained, individualized engagement that supports each student’s conceptual and professional development.
©Andrés Caballero, MFA 2026
How often do guest artists, curators, or critics visit for lectures and/or critiques?

The program hosts an ongoing visiting artist and scholar series (see above), bringing in nationally and internationally recognized practitioners for lectures, studio visits, and critiques throughout the academic year.
©Andrés Caballero, MFA 2026
How many students are admitted each year, and how many are photography focused?
2-3 students are accepted in the Photography, Video & Imaging Program (PVI) each year.
What is the approximate cohort size, and what effect does this have on critiques, collaboration, and networking?
Current PVI cohort size is 7 including 1st, 2nd, and 3rd year graduate students.
©Alexis Joy Hagestad, MFA 2026
What kind of work are current students creating?
PVI graduate students are nationally and internationally recognized for their work, receiving major fellowships, awards, and exhibition opportunities. From our most recent cohorts of students:
Beihua Guo – MFA 2027

Guo is an MFA candidate whose work investigates how histories are remembered, buried, or erased, particularly in landscapes marked by colonialism, extraction, and displacement. He has received numerous awards, including the Alexia, the Lucie Scholarship, the Aftermath Project, the Lenscratch Student Prize Honorable Mention, and was named a University of Arizona Graduate Fellow (2024–25). His work has been exhibited globally.
Andrés Caballero – MFA 2026

Caballero is a photographer and researcher whose work centers on borderlands communities and identity. A Fulbright scholar and Mellon-Fronteridades Graduate Fellow, he has participated in over 20 exhibitions and received more than 20 grants and fellowships during his MFA. He was named the College of Fine Arts Outstanding Graduate Student (2026).
Alexis Hagestad – MFA 2026

Hagestad’s interdisciplinary practice addresses wildfire ecology, climate change and memory. Her installation-based work has been exhibited in solo presentations, and she was awarded the Marcia Grand Centennial Sculpture Prize (2024), a major award dedicated to supporting an MFA candidate’s proposed project.
Camille Trautman – MFA 2025

Trautman is an artist whose work investigates indigenous identity, gender dysphoria, and mediated self-perception through the use of photography and video. Their work has been exhibited publicly, including a recent solo exhibition at the Frye Art Museum in Seattle Washington.
Marcus Xavier Cormicle – MFA 2028

Cormicle is a lens-based artist and curator whose work examines grief, family history, and Indigenous and Chicanx experience in the Southwest. He was awarded the 2025 United States Latinx Artist Fellowship and has completed multiple residencies, including Light Work and New Mexico Arts. His work extends into community-based curatorial practice.
Maya Jackson – MFA 2026

Jackson is an image-based artist working across photography, video, and installation, exploring black identity, memory, and the limits of photographic truth. She has exhibited work across regional and national venues and was selected as a University of Arizona Graduate Fellow (2023–24). She is the recipient of an Anderson Ranch Arts Center 2026 Workshop Scholarship in Photography and New Media and the 2025 University of Arizona College of Fine Arts Graduate Creative Achievement Award.
Lisa Elmaleh – MFA 2029

Elmaleh is an analog photographer, artist, and humanitarian. As a University of Arizona Graduate Fellow, she is expanding her most recent project Promised Land/Tierra Prometida that documents migration and humanitarian aid in the US-Mexico borderlands. She is the recipient of numerous awards, including a Guggenheim Fellowship, the Arnold Newman Prize, and the Puffin Foundation. Her work has been exhibited internationally.
Eduardo ‘Lalo’ Marroquin – MFA 2029

Marroquin centers his practice on 19th-century alternative photographic processes—specifically the albumen print—reclaiming a medium historically tied to Western colonial expansion to build counter-archives that center Mexican and queer identities historically excluded from the Western photographic canon. He holds a BFA in Studio Art from the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, trained under photography historian and artist Brenton Hamilton and was awarded Graduate Access Fellowship at U of A.
©Alexis Joy Hagestad, MFA 2026
What is the total cost of the program (and duration), and what funding options are available? Are there teaching assistantships, and what percentage of tuition do they cover?

Through Graduate Assistantships and other forms of aid, students are guaranteed 3 years of full funding. This includes the full cost of tuition (students are still responsible for university, program and course fees) plus a $10,000 annual stipend.
©Maya Jackson, MFA 2026
Are additional grants/resources available to support student projects?
Arts Research production support- Marcia Grand Centennial Award (10K), Helen Gross Award (2,500K)
Travel support- College of Fine Arts Small Grants, CFA Medici Awards (1K), Graduate Professional Student Council (GPSC, 1K) by proposal through the UA Graduate College.
Students are eligible for School of Art Endowed Scholarships (fall awards) 75K-100K awarded per year across the school (undergraduate and graduate).
©Maya Jackson, MFA 2026
What types of careers do alumni pursue, and how does the program support students after graduation?
Graduates pursue careers as exhibiting artists, educators, and cultural producers, supported by a strong alumni network.
©Beihua Guo, MFA Candidate
